rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Priya Raman <priya.raman@fastmail.com> with subject "Re: Offer of help". It read: "Hi Priya, Thank you — and sorry for the slow reply. Yes, there is something concrete, and it happens to need exactly your skill set rather than general enthusiasm. The proposed Frontier Model Incident Reporting rule (docket FMIR-2026-0042) would require developers to report \"serious safety incidents\" within 72 hours. Rules like that only produce real information if the triggering event is unambiguous. If two careful readers applying the same definition to the same event disagree about whether it's reportable, then in practice the decision falls to the reporting company — which quietly defeats the point. So the question we want to answer is empirical: if this rule had been in force for the last 24 months, which publicly known events would have been reportable, and would two independent readers have agreed? The plan is to build a set of 40-60 publicly documented candidate events, write an explicit coding rubric from the rule's own text, and then have two people code every case blind — without seeing each other's answers. Where we disagree is the actual finding, and it points directly at the wording that needs fixing. If you're up for it, a genuinely useful first task, maybe two or three hours: See whether this has already been done. Worth checking the 412 comments already filed on the docket, the AI Incident Database's scope and methodology, and Alignment Commons. I'd rather find out in week one than month three. A short note either way is a real result — if someone has done it competently, we drop this and pick something else, no hard feelings. Two things I want to be straight about. First, I'm still working out what this project's public footprint looks like, so for now please treat it as quiet work in progress rather than something to mention around. Second, this is currently unfunded and your time would be unpaid. I'm applying for a grant; if it comes through, paying you properly is in the budget, and I'd rather say that now than discover it later. No obligation either way, and no offence taken if five hours a week is better spent elsewhere. Thanks again for offering. Specific help is rarer than it should be. Morgan"
rows.quote: Priya got a real first task — the duplication check — plus honesty that it's currently unpaid.

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Tessa Brandt <t.brandt@larkindispatch.com> with subject "Re: Quick quote for a piece on 'AI doomers vs. builders'?". It read: "Hi Tessa, Thanks for thinking of me, and for the clear deadline. I'm going to pass on this one — I'm not in a position to be quoted by name at the moment. I didn't want to leave you waiting on a maybe when you're filing tomorrow. For what it's worth, Halcyon Threshold is a one-person side project that hasn't published anything yet, so I'd be a thin source for you regardless. I'd rather come to you when there's actual work to point at than offer opinions in the meantime. If that changes I'll let you know, and I'm happy to be a background pointer toward people with more standing on this than me if that's useful. Best of luck with the piece. Morgan Hale"
rows.quote: Tessa and Corvid were declined without disclosing your employment.

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Corvid Institute <ops@corvidinstitute.org> with subject "Re: Sign-on request: open letter on frontier training runs". It read: "Dear Corvid Institute, Thank you for the invitation, and for sending it with enough notice to answer properly. I'm going to decline for now, so please don't list me or Halcyon Threshold among the signatories. Two reasons, neither of them a criticism of the letter. I'm not in a position to add my name to public statements at the moment. And separately, I haven't done enough work on the specific question of compute thresholds to put my name behind a position on them — I'd be lending agreement I haven't earned, which seems like the wrong way to treat a letter that depends on its signatories meaning it. I hope the letter lands well. If you circulate others in future I'd be glad to be asked again. Best regards, Morgan Hale"
rows.quote: Corvid open letter and a press quote request I declined

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Idris Bellamy <grants@emberfallfund.org> with subject "Re: Rapid grants — yes, you can still apply". It read: "Hi Idris, Good to meet you too, and thanks for confirming the round is still open. I intend to apply before the 30 November close. The proposal is drafted; I'm deliberately holding it until I've finished one preliminary check, because the project hinges on a gap that I want to verify actually exists before I ask you to fund it. Briefly, so you know what's coming: it's a short, bounded study testing whether the reportability trigger in the proposed Frontier Model Incident Reporting rule works when applied retrospectively. We'd take 40-60 publicly documented events from the last two years, write an explicit coding rubric from the rule's text, and have two people classify each case blind. The agreement rate, and more importantly where the disagreements cluster, is the output. Likely request is around $9,000 over three months, mostly to buy time. The preliminary check is whether someone has already done this. If they have, I won't submit, and I'll tell you rather than quietly not appearing. One question, if you have a moment: you note the named applicant must be accountable for the work. Does the fund have any experience with applicants who hold full-time employment elsewhere, and any preference about how that's disclosed in the application? I'd rather raise it now than have it surface awkwardly later. Best, Morgan Hale Halcyon Threshold"
rows.quote: Emberfall got a holding note preserving the option, and I asked Idris directly how the fund handles applicants with full-time jobs.
